text: After these things, when King Ahasuerus' rage had subsided, he remembered Vashti — what she had done, and what had been decreed against her.
Then the king's attendants who served him said, "Let a search be made for beautiful young virgins for the king.

Let the king appoint officers in every province of his kingdom to gather every beautiful young virgin to the citadel of Susa, to the harem, under the care of Hegai, the king's eunuch who keeps the women, and let their beauty treatments be provided.
And let the young woman who pleases the king become queen in place of Vashti." The proposal pleased the king, and he acted on it.
Now there was a Jew in the citadel of Susa named Mordecai son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite,
who had been carried away from Jerusalem among the exiles taken with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried into exile.

He was raising Hadassah, that is, Esther, his uncle's daughter, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman was lovely in form and beautiful to look at, and when her father and mother died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter.

versions.text: He was raising Hadassah, that is, Esther, his uncle's daughter, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman was shapely and beautiful, and when her father and mother died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew pairs two expressions — beauty of form and beauty of appearance. "Shapely" carries a modern, somewhat coarse connotation in English and flattens the pairing; "lovely in form and beautiful to look at" is closer to the Hebrew and reads better aloud.

text: So when the king's order and decree were proclaimed and many young women were gathered to the citadel of Susa under Hegai's care, Esther too was taken to the king's palace, into the care of Hegai, keeper of the women.

The young woman pleased him and won his favor, so he quickly provided her with her beauty treatments and her portions of food, along with seven chosen maids from the king's palace, and he moved her and her maids to the best place in the harem.
Esther had not disclosed her people or her family background, for Mordecai had ordered her not to tell.
Day after day Mordecai walked back and forth in front of the courtyard of the harem, to learn how Esther was and what was happening to her.

Now when the turn came for each young woman to go in to King Ahasuerus, she had first completed the twelve months prescribed for the women — for so their time of beautifying was filled: six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with perfumes and women's cosmetics.

versions.text: Each young woman's turn came to go in to King Ahasuerus after she had completed twelve months of treatment prescribed for the women: six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with perfumes and women's cosmetics.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew opens with a temporal clause ("when the turn came...") that leads into verse 13, and it includes the explanatory line "for so the days of their beautifying were completed," which is dropped in the current rendering.

text: When the young woman went in to the king in this way, whatever she asked for was given her to take with her from the harem to the king's palace.

In the evening she would go in, and in the morning she would return to the second harem, under the care of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch who kept the concubines. She would not go in to the king again unless he delighted in her and summoned her by name.

versions.text: In the evening she would go in, and in the morning she would return to a second harem, under the care of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch who kept the concubines. She would not go in to the king again unless he delighted in her and summoned her by name.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew refers to a specific, known second house of the women, so the definite article "the second harem" is more accurate than the indefinite "a second harem."

text: When the turn came for Esther, the daughter of Abihail, the uncle of Mordecai who had taken her as his own daughter, to go in to the king, she asked for nothing except what Hegai, the king's eunuch who kept the women, advised. And Esther won the admiration of everyone who saw her.
Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus, into his royal residence, in the tenth month, the month of Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign.
The king loved Esther more than all the other women, and she won his favor and devotion more than all the other virgins. So he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen in place of Vashti.
Then the king gave a great banquet for all his officials and servants — Esther's banquet. He granted the provinces a remission of taxes and distributed gifts with royal generosity.
When the virgins were gathered a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate.
Esther still had not disclosed her family background or her people, just as Mordecai had ordered her; she did what Mordecai told her, as she had done when he was raising her.
In those days, while Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the threshold, grew angry and plotted to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.
But the plot became known to Mordecai, and he told Queen Esther, and Esther reported it to the king in Mordecai's name.

The matter was investigated and confirmed, and the two men were hanged on a pole.[^1]

[^1]: Or "impaled on a stake"; the Hebrew word means "tree" or "wood."

versions.text: The matter was investigated and confirmed, and the two men were hanged on a gallows. And it was recorded in the book of the chronicles in the king's presence.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew term simply means "tree/wood," and the Persian practice was likely impalement or exposure on a pole rather than hanging on a modern-style gallows. A brief footnote helps the reader without changing the familiar rendering.
